questions.q: What does inferSchema=True do when reading the taxi_zone_lookup.csv file?
options: Has Spark scan the file to guess real column types, instead of treating every column as a string by default
Automatically removes duplicate rows
Forces every column to be read as a string
Only applies to Parquet files, not CSV
questions.explain: Without it, Spark's CSV reader defaults to treating all columns as strings even when they're clearly numeric.

questions.q: Why does combining two filter conditions require & (and |) instead of Python's and/or?
options: Each side is a column expression evaluated per-row, not a single boolean value, which & and | are designed to combine
PySpark does not support filtering on more than one condition
and/or only work with string columns in PySpark
& is required only when using inferSchema=True
questions.explain: col("a") > 0 and col("b") > 0 would try to evaluate a Column object as a single Python boolean, which fails/behaves incorrectly.

questions.q: What does withColumn() do when given a name that already exists in the DataFrame?
options: It replaces that existing column with the new expression
It raises an error and stops the script
It silently does nothing
It renames the DataFrame itself
questions.explain: If the name is new, withColumn() adds it; if it already exists, it replaces that column in place.

questions.q: What is the difference between na.drop() and na.fill()?
options: na.drop() removes rows missing a required field entirely, while na.fill() substitutes a default value instead of dropping the row
They are two names for the exact same operation
na.drop() only works on numeric columns
na.fill() deletes the entire DataFrame
questions.explain: Which to use depends on the field — dropping rows with no fare_amount may make sense, while filling a missing passenger_count with 1 might be safer than discarding the row.

questions.q: Why use col("fare_amount") instead of trips.fare_amount in a filter?
options: col() isn't tied to one specific DataFrame variable, which matters once you're working with columns from more than one DataFrame, such as in a join
trips.fare_amount is invalid PySpark syntax
col() is required for every single PySpark operation with no exceptions
There is no functional difference in any situation
questions.explain: trips.fare_amount only works for columns that actually belong to the trips DataFrame; col() is more flexible once multiple DataFrames are involved.
